mcqs.question: Why is the database usually the first bottleneck at traffic scale, ahead of the app tier?
options: Because a stateless app tier clones cheaply and adds capacity nearly linearly, while a single database's connection count and CPU don't scale the same way
Because databases are inherently slower software than application servers
Because load balancers cannot route traffic to more than a handful of app servers
Because databases always run on older hardware than app servers
mcqs.explanation: The asymmetry is architectural: adding app servers is cheap and near-linear once they're stateless, but the database is a shared, stateful resource whose connection and CPU ceilings don't move just by adding more app servers. It isn't about raw software speed, load-balancer limits, or hardware age.

mcqs.question: After adding read replicas to fix connection exhaustion, what typically becomes the next bottleneck?
options: The load balancer, which cannot support more than one replica
Replication lag causing replica reads to return stale data under heavier write volume
mcqs.explanation: Read replicas relieve connection pressure but introduce a new axis of risk: as write volume grows, replicas can fall further behind, so reads that assumed fresh data start surfacing staleness bugs. Load balancers scale to many replicas fine; client bandwidth and app-tier memory aren't the mechanism here.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't adding read replicas help a write-heavy workload the way it helps a read-heavy one?
options: Every write still has to land on the primary — replicas only add read capacity, not write capacity
Replicas actually make writes slower than having no replicas at all
Write-heavy workloads don't exist in practice at scale
Replicas can accept writes just as well as the primary, so this isn't actually a real distinction
mcqs.explanation: Read replicas copy data from the primary; they don't accept writes themselves (in the common async-replica setup), so a write-heavy workload gets no relief from adding more of them — the fix there is sharding or partitioning writes. Replicas don't slow writes down, and write-heavy workloads are extremely common at scale.

mcqs.question: A candidate immediately proposes "add a cache" for a scaling problem. Why is that a weak first move?
options: Caches only ever work for static assets, never for database rows
Caches always cost more than scaling the database directly
A cache only helps if the bottleneck is genuinely read-heavy and cacheable — it does nothing for write-throughput or connection-leak problems, and adds complexity if applied blindly
Adding a cache is illegal under most cloud providers' terms of service
mcqs.explanation: "Add a cache" is a fix for a specific diagnosis — read-heavy, cacheable load — not a universal answer. Applied to a write-heavy bottleneck or an app-tier connection leak, it adds complexity without addressing the actual saturated resource. It isn't limited to static assets, isn't inherently costlier, and isn't a legal issue.
